paragraphs: Topic models describe documents as mixtures of topics, with each topic represented by a distribution over words. Recovering those distributions is computationally difficult in general. This paper develops an approach based on singular value decomposition, or SVD, that provides a recovery guarantee under assumptions about topic vocabulary and the mixtures appearing in documents.

The vocabulary assumption uses groups of topic-specific catchwords. These words occur more frequently in their associated topic than in any other individual topic, and their combined frequency matters more than each word being common alone. The document assumption requires dominant admixtures: one topic contributes substantially more than the others. A crucial thresholding step prepares the data before SVD.

Under these assumptions, the algorithm recovers topics with bounded total absolute error in their word probabilities. Its sample requirement has nearly optimal dependence on how rarely a topic is dominant. Evidence from several real corpora supports the assumptions, and the reported experiments substantially outperform the compared state of the art. The guarantee is therefore tied to a specified corpus structure, while the experiments support its practical relevance.
neurips-2014-a-provable-svd-based-algori.tldr: An SVD-based topic learner provides bounded-error recovery when documents have dominant topics and topic-specific groups of catchwords.

paragraphs: Social choice concerns decisions made on behalf of multiple agents. This paper frames that task as statistical decision-making: specify a model of rankings, a set of possible decisions, and a loss describing how costly each decision would be for a given underlying parameter. A social choice mechanism then becomes a rule for minimizing expected loss.

This perspective makes the intended decision and its consequences explicit in the design of a voting or ranking rule. The authors compare Bayesian estimators for the Mallows and Condorcet ranking models with the Kemeny rule. They examine normative properties alongside computational complexity and behavior as the amount of data grows.

The Bayesian estimator for the Condorcet model satisfies anonymity, neutrality, and monotonicity, and can be computed in polynomial time. For some ground-truth parameters, when observations come from the Condorcet model, its asymptotic behavior differs from both alternatives. Thus, even with abundant data, the choice of statistical decision rule can matter. The framework provides a way to analyze that choice through explicit modeling assumptions and losses.
neurips-2014-a-statistical-decision-theo.tldr: The paper designs and compares social choice rules as statistical decisions that minimize expected loss.

paragraphs: Kernel-based hypothesis tests use representations of probability distributions to ask questions such as whether two samples come from the same distribution or whether variables are independent. This paper addresses their use with random processes, including time series. In that setting, a naive permutation bootstrap can fail, so choosing an appropriate resampling procedure is essential.

The proposed wild bootstrap supports a broad class of tests built from V-statistics. The relevant statistics are degenerate under the null hypothesis and non-degenerate away from it, making their behavior under the null central to the method. The authors use the procedure to construct tests with provable consistency for the random-process setting.

They demonstrate the approach through a two-sample test, an instantaneous independence test, and a test of independence across multiple time lags. Experiments report strong performance on synthetic examples, audio data, and benchmarking of the Gibbs sampler. The contribution combines a theoretical justification for this class of dependent-data tests with examples showing how the same resampling idea serves several testing tasks.
neurips-2014-a-wild-bootstrap-for-degene.tldr: A wild bootstrap enables provably consistent kernel tests for random processes where naive permutation resampling fails.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet allocation represents an object, such as a text or image, as a mixture of hidden topics. This paper studies how variational Bayesian learning affects sparsity in that model. Sparsity concerns how strongly the learned representation concentrates on a smaller set of components, making it relevant to the structure of the resulting topic mixtures.

The authors analytically derive the leading term of the variational Bayesian free energy in an asymptotic setting. Their analysis identifies thresholds in the Dirichlet hyperparameters around which sparsity-inducing behavior changes sharply. These parameters therefore influence more than a gradual adjustment in the solution: crossing a threshold can substantially alter the tendency toward sparse representations.

The analysis also finds that variational Bayes tends to induce weaker sparsity than maximum a posteriori estimation in LDA, reversing the relationship observed in other models. Experiments on real Last.FM music data support the practical validity of the asymptotic theory. The result shows why expectations about the sparsity of an inference method must account for the particular model in which it is used.
neurips-2014-analysis-of-variational-bay.tldr: An asymptotic analysis finds sparsity transitions in LDA and shows that variational Bayes tends to produce weaker sparsity than MAP.

paragraphs: Constrained optimization can proceed by adding constraints as they become needed, an idea used in cutting-plane methods. This paper investigates a similar augmentative strategy within message passing for integral solutions. It considers two combinatorial tasks: finding a traveling-salesman tour and partitioning a graph into communities through modularity optimization.

For the traveling-salesman problem, the authors construct a factor graph from the Held–Karp formulation. It contains exponentially many constraint factors, whose tables are also exponential in size but sparse. For graph partitioning, they introduce binary variables and many constraints enforcing clique formation. Despite these large constraint descriptions, they derive simple message updates for both problems.

Benchmark experiments produce competitive solutions. In the traveling-salesman experiments, the method finds near-optimal tours with running time observed to grow cubically with problem size. That scaling is an empirical finding, rather than a general worst-case guarantee. The results support the practical viability of combining augmentation with message passing even when an explicit description of all constraints would be very large.
neurips-2014-augmentative-message-passin.tldr: Adding constraints within message passing yields competitive graph partitions and empirically near-optimal traveling-salesman tours.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a family of graphical models that combines nonparametric trees with more richly connected components called blossoms. The goal is to describe a high-dimensional joint distribution while retaining efficient estimation and evaluation. The construction brings together the flexibility of nonparametric tree relationships and methods associated with Gaussian graphical models.

Tree edges are selected to connect variables whose relationships most strongly violate joint Gaussianity. The remaining edges are divided into disjoint groups and assigned to tree nodes using a nonparametric partial-correlation statistic. Each group then becomes a nonparanormal blossom, with an arbitrary graph learned using established graphical-lasso methods.

The final distribution factorizes according to the combined tree branches and blossoms. This arrangement gives the model a way to represent relationships beyond a tree while preserving a structured joint density that can be efficiently estimated and evaluated at test points. The paper supplies theoretical properties and experiments on simulated and real data supporting the effectiveness of the construction. Its central contribution is this combination of complementary forms of dependency modeling.
neurips-2014-blossom-tree-graphical-mode.tldr: Blossom trees combine nonparametric tree relationships with richer graphical components to efficiently model high-dimensional distributions.

paragraphs: Distributing machine-learning optimization across computers creates a cost beyond the calculations themselves: the computers must communicate. This paper treats that communication as a major performance bottleneck. It introduces COCOA, a framework that uses local computation to substantially reduce the communication required during distributed optimization.

COCOA operates in a primal-dual setting, connecting the original optimization problem with its dual formulation. The key design choice is to make productive use of computation performed locally, so progress requires less information exchange across the distributed system. The authors provide a strong convergence-rate analysis for the resulting class of algorithms, giving theoretical support to the framework.

They also implement the approach in Spark and test it on real-world distributed datasets. In those experiments, COCOA reaches the same 0.001-accurate solution quality an average of 25 times faster than the compared state-of-the-art mini-batch SGD and SDCA methods. This is an experimental average for the reported comparisons. It illustrates how reducing communication can translate into substantially faster optimization while maintaining the target solution quality.
neurips-2014-communication-efficient-dis.tldr: COCOA uses local primal-dual computation to reduce communication and achieves a reported average 25-fold speedup in distributed experiments.

paragraphs: An object's appearance can vary with pose or deformation while its identity stays the same. This paper represents such identity-preserving changes through symmetry groups: collections of transformations that can be composed. It extends the idea behind convolutional feature maps, which organize responses over translations, to feature maps defined over arbitrary symmetry groups.

The resulting deep symmetry networks use kernel-based interpolation to share parameters and pool responses across symmetry spaces of any dimension in a tractable way. They are trained with backpropagation. Across layers, the composition of feature transformations provides a way to build deep representations that explicitly reflect the chosen symmetries.

Experiments on NORB and MNIST-rot use symmetry networks over the affine group. The reported results show substantially lower sample complexity than convolutional networks, attributed to better capture of the data's symmetries. This supports the idea that representing relevant transformations directly can reduce the amount of training data required in these settings. The experimental finding concerns the tested affine-group networks, while the proposed architecture has a broader formulation.
neurips-2014-deep-symmetry-networks-308c.tldr: Deep symmetry networks extend convolutional feature maps to symmetry groups and reduce sample complexity in the reported affine-group experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model means estimating a structured description of relationships among variables. In high-dimensional settings, classical maximum-likelihood estimation can break down. This paper studies the precise form of that failure and uses it to construct simple estimators for sparse graphical models expressed as exponential-family distributions.

The method first applies a carefully designed backward map that is well-defined and available in closed form. It then uses thresholding to enforce the intended sparsity structure. This separates the estimation procedure into a direct calculation and a sparsification step, providing a computationally simpler alternative to solving an optimization problem for an l1-regularized maximum-likelihood estimate.

The statistical analysis shows that these elementary estimators achieve the same asymptotic convergence rates as the more computationally demanding regularized estimators. Matching rates concerns how estimation error scales asymptotically; it does not assert identical estimates. Simulations involving both discrete and Gaussian graphical models support the statistical findings and show substantial computational advantages. The contribution demonstrates that a carefully constructed direct estimator can retain strong statistical performance.
neurips-2014-elementary-estimators-for-g.tldr: Closed-form maps followed by thresholding estimate sparse graphical models with convergence rates matching l1-regularized maximum likelihood.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to recover the sparsest vector contained in a given subspace. Such a vector has relatively few nonzero entries, and finding it is relevant to sparse dictionary learning, sparse PCA, and other signal-processing problems. The challenge is to recover this structure from the subspace containing it.

For a subspace of dimension n, simple convex heuristics provably break down when the target's fraction of nonzero entries substantially exceeds 1 divided by the square root of n. The authors propose a relatively simple nonconvex method based on alternating directions. Their analysis establishes recovery with a constant-order fraction of nonzero entries, reaching the linear sparsity scaling emphasized in the title.

That guarantee assumes a planted sparse model: the desired sparse vector is embedded in an otherwise random subspace. The assumption is central to the theoretical result. Experiments also show success on more challenging data models arising from sparse dictionary learning. Together, the analysis and experiments identify a setting where a practical nonconvex method goes beyond the stated recovery range of simple convex heuristics.
neurips-2014-finding-a-sparse-vector-in-.tldr: A nonconvex alternating-directions method provably recovers vectors with linear sparsity under a planted sparse-subspace model.

paragraphs: Generative models of objects benefit from inputs that center and align the object of interest. Large scenes make that difficult because the object appears alongside background clutter. This paper introduces a deep-learning framework that uses visual attention to send information from a selected scene region into an aligned, canonical representation for generative modeling.

The attention mechanism lets the generative model focus its resources on the object rather than the surrounding scene. Posterior inference uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, with a convolutional neural network supplying good starting points. The framework therefore combines attention, a generative representation, and learned initialization for its inference procedure.

The reported results focus on faces. After learning face images, the model can robustly attend to face regions belonging to previously unseen test subjects. It can also learn generative models of new faces from a separate dataset of large images without known face locations. These findings support the use of attention to connect scene-level inputs with object-centered generative learning, including a setting where object positions are not supplied.
neurips-2014-learning-generative-models-.tldr: An attention-based generative framework learns face models from large images even when face locations are unknown.

paragraphs: Summarizing an image collection requires selecting images that together make a useful summary. This paper learns a scoring function for that selection by combining submodular functions. The authors identify submodularity in several previously used scoring functions and introduce function classes addressing coverage, likelihood, and diversity.

They formulate summary selection as supervised learning through large-margin structured prediction. This allows the mixture of scoring functions to be learned from examples of summaries. The contribution therefore connects desirable properties of an image summary with a training procedure for deciding how those properties should contribute to its score.

The paper also introduces V-ROUGE, an automatic evaluation measure for image summaries, and a dataset of 14 real-world collections with many human-created reference summaries gathered through Mechanical Turk. On this new dataset, the learned approach outperforms all compared methods. The authors describe the combined modeling, evaluation, and dataset contribution as, to their knowledge, the first systematic approach to quantifying this problem. The reported performance advantage is specific to the new dataset and its comparisons.
neurips-2014-learning-mixtures-of-submod.tldr: Learned mixtures of submodular scoring functions improve image-collection summaries on a new dataset with human references.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification makes stored examples central to prediction, so compressing the sample raises an important question: what guarantees remain after reducing the examples used? This paper presents what the authors identify as the first nearest-neighbor sample-compression algorithm with nontrivial performance guarantees. It treats compression as a problem requiring theoretical justification as well as a procedure.

The authors accompany the algorithm's guarantees with hardness lower bounds that almost match them. These two parts serve different purposes: the algorithm establishes what can be achieved, while the lower bounds establish barriers to improvement. Their close agreement supports the description of the resulting bound as nearly optimal.

The analysis also gives new insight into margin-based nearest-neighbor classification in metric spaces, sharpening and simplifying existing bounds. This connects the compression result with the role of separation in classification problems defined through distances. The paper includes encouraging empirical results as well. Its central finding is the combination of a guaranteed compression algorithm and nearly matching hardness evidence, with experiments providing additional practical support.
neurips-2014-near-optimal-sample-compres.tldr: A nearest-neighbor sample-compression algorithm comes with performance guarantees and almost matching hardness bounds.

paragraphs: Lifted inference exploits symmetry in a first-order probabilistic model to reduce a large inference problem to a smaller one. This paper introduces two rules for maximum a posteriori, or MAP, inference in Markov logic networks. The goal is to recover the most probable assignment while working with a reduced model whenever the rules apply.

The first rule uses a defined structure called a single-occurrence equivalence class of logical variables. Variables in these classes can be replaced by domain constants in a smaller network from which the original MAP assignment can be recovered. The second rule permits removing certain formulas when every remaining variable equivalence class is single-occurrence and the removed formulas are true at extreme assignments, where each predicate's groundings share a truth value.

The authors prove both rules sound, so the reductions have a formal justification under their stated conditions. A detailed experimental evaluation reports better scalability and MAP solution quality than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution expands the structural situations in which symmetry can simplify MAP inference.
neurips-2014-new-rules-for-domain-indepe.tldr: Two sound lifting rules reduce qualifying Markov logic networks and improve MAP inference in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Robust PCA seeks to separate a low-rank matrix from sparse corruptions. The low-rank component captures shared structure, while the sparse component accounts for perturbations affecting relatively few entries. This paper proposes a nonconvex recovery method that alternates projections onto low-rank and sparse matrix sets, with denoising steps between them.

The authors prove correct recovery under tight conditions matching those used by state-of-the-art convex relaxations. The importance of this result is that the simpler nonconvex procedure retains a formal recovery guarantee in the stated setting. The analysis also provides a global convergence guarantee, a notable property for a method operating over nonconvex sets.

For an m-by-n matrix with m at least n, the stated runtime is O(r²mn log(1/epsilon)), where r is the recovered rank and epsilon is the target accuracy. The abstract contrasts this with O(mn²/epsilon) for convex relaxation methods. Its runtime nearly matches ordinary PCA, apart from an additional rank factor. Thus, the proposed method combines conditional recovery guarantees with a computational cost much closer to standard PCA.
neurips-2014-non-convex-robust-pca-2e2e6.tldr: Alternating low-rank and sparse projections provide provable robust PCA recovery with runtime close to ordinary PCA.

paragraphs: Matching local visual features depends strongly on the similarity measure used to compare them. A hand-designed measure may fit the data poorly, while learning one can introduce restrictive parameterizations or high computational costs. This paper proposes Quantized Kernels as a flexible family of nonlinear similarities intended to make learning tractable.

The method defines kernels over the indices produced by a data quantizer. In the original feature space, this makes similarity piecewise constant: comparisons depend on the quantized representations. Quantization also compresses the features, connecting the representation used for storage with the space in which the similarity function is learned.

On a standard benchmark, the authors report state-of-the-art matching performance while using only a few bits per feature dimension. The kernels also admit explicit, nonlinear, low-dimensional feature mappings, providing access to Euclidean geometry for uncompressed features. These results show two useful aspects of the same construction: compact representations for matching and explicit feature mappings for geometric operations. The performance claim refers to the benchmark evaluated in the paper.
neurips-2014-quantized-kernel-learning-f.tldr: Quantized Kernels learn nonlinear feature similarities while compressing descriptors, achieving strong benchmark matching with few bits per dimension.

paragraphs: Processing every pixel of a large image can make convolutional networks expensive. This paper proposes a recurrent model that gathers information by choosing a sequence of locations or regions. Only the selected regions receive high-resolution processing, allowing the amount of computation to be controlled independently of the input image's size.

The model adaptively decides where to look as it processes an image or video. It has a built-in degree of translation invariance, and its attention policy is specific to the task. Because the model is non-differentiable, the authors train it using reinforcement-learning methods, connecting useful visual decisions with the policy that selects the observations.

On image-classification tasks, the model significantly outperforms a convolutional-network baseline for cluttered images. In a dynamic visual-control problem, it learns to track a simple object without an explicit tracking signal. These findings show that selective visual processing can support both recognition and control in the tested settings. The tracking result also indicates that a useful attention behavior can emerge without being directly specified as the training target.
neurips-2014-recurrent-models-of-visual-.tldr: A recurrent attention model learns where to look, improving cluttered-image recognition and learning object tracking without explicit tracking supervision.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether learning a nonlinear representation can take time comparable to linear learning. Its proposed algorithm begins with a base linear representation and explicitly expands it with higher-order interaction features. The objective is to gain the expressive value of interactions while keeping computation central to the design.

The expansion is adaptive, so the representation is developed through the algorithm rather than described only as a fixed linear feature set. Interaction features make combinations of base features available to the learner. This is the source of the method's nonlinear representation, and its explicit construction makes feature expansion the central mechanism of the approach.

An extensive experimental study reports a very favorable tradeoff between computation and predictive performance against strong baselines. The stated finding supports the algorithm as an efficient way to obtain useful nonlinear representations in the evaluated settings. The motivating question about matching linear learning's cost remains a design goal rather than a universal runtime guarantee in the abstract; the reported evidence concerns the quality of the empirical computation–prediction tradeoff.
neurips-2014-scalable-non-linear-learnin.tldr: Adaptive expansion of higher-order feature interactions produces a favorable empirical tradeoff between computation and predictive performance.

paragraphs: Markov logic networks describe large probabilistic networks through compact, weighted logical templates. Lifted inference tries to work with those templates without expanding every instance. Complex structure and observed evidence can break the symmetries that make this possible, forcing existing methods to ground much of the network and reducing their scalability.

This paper proposes lifted importance sampling that never grounds the entire network. It addresses both expensive parts of importance sampling: generating samples and computing their weights. An informed proposal distribution comes from a compressed network representation and is easy to sample. Weight computation visits only a small subset of sampled groundings for each formula instead of all possible groundings.

The authors show that the resulting estimate is asymptotically unbiased. This qualification concerns its limiting behavior, rather than guaranteeing an unbiased answer from any finite run. Experiments on several Markov logic networks demonstrate promise for the approach. The contribution is a coordinated way to reduce the cost of both sampling and weighting while maintaining a formal asymptotic property.
neurips-2014-scaling-up-importance-sampl.tldr: Compressed proposals and selective weight computation enable asymptotically unbiased importance sampling without fully grounding a Markov logic network.

paragraphs: Particle-collision measurements are incomplete and imprecise, making statistical analysis essential to identifying rare physical processes. This paper studies neural networks for detecting Higgs boson decays to tau leptons. The authors train their models using a dataset containing 82 million simulated collision events.

The approach addresses a feature-design problem in high-energy physics. Analysts commonly devote substantial effort to constructing high-level variables from raw collider measurements to improve statistical power. The paper investigates deep neural networks' ability to discover useful high-level features automatically, making representation learning part of the detection procedure.

The reported findings indicate that deep architectures are particularly well suited to this task and can increase discovery significance. Their value lies in learning informative structure from the data for distinguishing the decay process of interest. The evidence comes from the simulated-event study described in the abstract, so the result concerns improved analysis for this search task rather than a reported experimental discovery. It supports learned features as a way to strengthen the statistical use of collider measurements.
neurips-2014-searching-for-higgs-boson-d.tldr: Deep networks learn useful features from simulated collider events and improve significance for detecting Higgs decays to tau leptons.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can express nonlinear predictors through a feature space that may be infinite-dimensional. This paper proposes a Sparse Random Feature algorithm that minimizes an l1-regularized objective in the Hilbert space induced by a kernel. The goal is to learn a nonlinear predictor with a sparse representation.

The authors interpret random-feature learning as randomized coordinate descent in that infinite-dimensional space. Their analysis shows convergence to a solution comparable to the exact kernel method within epsilon precision using O(1/epsilon) random features. This contrasts with the O(1/epsilon²)-type dependence obtained through the Monte Carlo analyses discussed in the abstract, giving a different theoretical account of random-feature efficiency.

In regression and classification experiments, the algorithm produces sparse solutions that use less memory and prediction time while maintaining comparable performance. It also reaches better solutions than a boosting approach when boosting's greedy step cannot be performed exactly. That comparison is conditional on inexact greedy optimization. The paper thus combines a convergence argument with evidence that sparsity can improve the practical cost of prediction.
neurips-2014-sparse-random-feature-algor.tldr: Viewing sparse random-feature learning as coordinate descent yields improved feature-count bounds and compact predictors in experiments.

paragraphs: Action videos contain spatial and temporal structure that low-level features may characterize inadequately. This paper represents actions through higher-level attributes, such as moving forward during a jump or being in the air. It considers both attributes supplied by people and attributes learned from data using dictionary-learning methods.

A large attribute vocabulary can contain noise and redundancy, making its representation variable and unnecessarily large. The authors therefore select a compact subset of discriminative attributes. They introduce three selection criteria and formulate the resulting problem as submodular optimization. A greedy algorithm comes with a guarantee of achieving at least a 1−1/e fraction of the optimum.

That guarantee concerns the attribute-selection objective. Recognition performance is assessed separately through experiments on Olympic Sports and UCF101. The results show substantial improvements to action-recognition algorithms and performance exceeding most of the recently proposed approaches considered. The paper's contribution links a high-level representation of actions with principled subset selection, using a theoretical approximation result to support selection and experiments to establish its recognition benefits.
neurips-2014-submodular-attribute-select.tldr: Submodular selection produces compact action-attribute representations with an approximation guarantee and improved video-recognition results.

paragraphs: Case-based reasoning explains observations through representative examples. The Bayesian Case Model brings that idea into a Bayesian generative framework for classification and clustering. It learns prototypes: actual observations that serve as characteristic representatives of clusters, making the representation directly connected to examples in the dataset.

The model jointly infers cluster labels, prototypes, and important features. It also learns subspaces, meaning sets of features that matter for characterizing each prototype. This pursues sparsity while allowing an explanation to identify both a representative case and the aspects of that case that are relevant to its cluster.

The paper reports quantitative interpretability benefits while preserving classification accuracy. In human-subject experiments, explanations generated by the model lead to statistically significant improvements in participants' understanding compared with explanations from prior methods. These findings support the combined use of prototypes and selected features as an understandable representation. The contribution is therefore both a probabilistic modeling framework and an experimentally supported approach to explaining its learned groups through concrete cases.
neurips-2014-the-bayesian-case-model-a-g.tldr: The Bayesian Case Model learns representative examples and relevant features, improving human understanding while preserving classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Sparse matrix factorization seeks factors with limited numbers of nonzero entries. This paper introduces a convex formulation based on a new atomic norm, assuming those numbers are fixed and known. Potential applications include sparse PCA with multiple factors, subspace clustering, and low-rank sparse bilinear regression.

The authors derive slow rates and bound the norm's statistical dimension for rank-one matrices. They report a statistical dimension an order of magnitude smaller than that of the usual l1 norm, trace norm, and their combinations. This theoretical comparison concerns rank-one matrices and indicates the value of designing a norm specifically around the assumed sparse-factor structure.

Convexity does not make this formulation computationally easy: the problem remains theoretically hard, and the paper does not obtain a provably polynomial-time solution scheme. Instead, the authors propose an active-set algorithm that exploits the convex problem's structure and report promising numerical results. The contribution therefore combines a statistically attractive formulation with a practical algorithm, while explicitly retaining a distinction between its statistical properties and computational guarantees.
neurips-2014-tight-convex-relaxations-fo.tldr: A new atomic norm improves rank-one statistical-dimension bounds for sparse factorization, although solving the convex formulation remains theoretically hard.

paragraphs: Column sampling selects a small, informative subset of a dataset for representation. Earlier structural approaches fit data with clusters, simplices, or convex hulls. This paper studies nonconvex hulls, aiming to select representatives that reflect more complex data structure through a hull adapted to the observations.

The proposed Zeta Hulls framework uses a graph-theoretic measure based on cycles to characterize structural complexity. A greedy algorithm uses this measure for structured column sampling. The graph structure therefore guides which data points enter the selected representation, connecting the sampling procedure to the geometry the method seeks to capture.

Pursuing a Zeta hull requires matrix inversion, creating a computational and storage cost. The authors accelerate that step through a low-rank approximation of the graph adjacency matrix, built with an efficient anchor-graph technique. Extensive experiments show that the resulting representations can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on text and image classification tasks. These findings support the practical usefulness of the nonconvex representation together with the approximation used to make its computation more manageable.
neurips-2014-zeta-hull-pursuits-learning.tldr: Zeta Hulls use graph cycles to select informative data subsets and learn nonconvex representations with strong classification results.
